title: Alpha-helix structural modeling
research_question: What polypeptide-chain configurations satisfy the best-established local chemical geometry and hydrogen-bonding constraints?
context: A structural chemistry program developed by Pauling and collaborators over many years, with a key paper-modeling episode in Oxford in March 1948 and formal publication with Robert B. Corey and H. R. Branson in 1951.
known_at_the_time: The group had accumulated accurate crystal-structure measurements of amino acids, peptides and related compounds specifically to establish interatomic distances, bond angles and other configurational parameters for polypeptide chains.
The peptide group was treated as strongly constrained and approximately planar, sharply limiting admissible local conformations.
Hydrogen bonding supplied an additional structural constraint on candidate chain configurations.
Contemporary fiber-diffraction work, especially Astbury's keratin patterns, prominently featured an approximately 5.1 A repeat that many investigators treated as a structural target.
unknown_at_the_time: Whether the 5.1 A repeat was a universal local constraint on individual polypeptide-chain helices rather than a higher-order packing effect.
The later breadth of alpha-helix occurrence across protein structures.
Later high-resolution structural confirmations and the full role of coiled-coil packing.
trigger_or_anomaly: The global protein-structure problem admitted many candidate folds, while a small set of local chemical constraints was much better established. Pauling's 1948 paper model produced a chemically plausible helix but its roughly 5.4 A pitch conflicted with the widely cited 5.1 A diffraction repeat.

alternatives_considered.option: Force the candidate helix to reproduce the 5.1 A repeat as an obligatory local periodicity.
alternatives_considered.outcome: Not adopted as the controlling constraint; publication was delayed while the discrepancy remained unresolved.

alternatives_considered.option: Use broader model families that relaxed peptide-group planarity or imposed integral residues per turn.
alternatives_considered.outcome: The Pauling-Corey-Branson approach instead privileged established chemical geometry and equivalent-residue helical construction.

decision_action: Preserve the best-established local bond geometry and peptide-group constraints, physically explore foldable chain configurations, and search for internally hydrogen-bonded helices without forcing an integer number of residues per turn. Treat the 5.1 A mismatch as unresolved rather than deforming the local chemistry to fit it, then publish after new synthetic-polypeptide evidence weakened the claim that the 5.1 A reflection was universal.
observed_result: The 1951 publication proposed two precise hydrogen-bonded helices, including the alpha helix. Subsequent diffraction work strongly supported the alpha-helix prediction and it became a foundational protein structural motif.
alternative_interpretations: The success cannot be attributed to a single heuristic alone; long-term crystallographic measurement, resonance theory, collaboration, physical model-building skill and later experimental evidence all contributed.
The famous 1948 paper-folding episode is partly reconstructed from retrospective testimony and archival synthesis; it should not be mistaken for a complete contemporaneous lab record.
notes: Golden Set v0.2: the primary 1951 publication and Pauling's 10 May 1984 Caltech oral history are now inspected, and the 5.1/5.4 A discrepancy is anchored in OSU archival synthesis. Still requires direct inspection of contemporaneous 1948 notes/drawings/correspondence before upgrading to high confidence.
